cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T3 answers T2's 'both are guesses' and turns it back on the raise.
cells.limitation: T7 and T11 open fresh threads without answering T6's test-the-work or T10's plan.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T9 adds that a review date isn't neutral once routines set; T10 builds exit conditions on it.
cells.limitation: T11's motive thread arrives late and T12 leaves it undeveloped.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T4 reframes the money-for-hours trade as a question about the next five years.
cells.limitation: Health, sleep and family time appear only in Section E, never debated.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T6 accepts T5's testing and extends it from the route to the work itself.
cells.limitation: T4's wrong-ledger challenge never reshapes the Bias Auditor's later turns.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D: the percentage is the least informative number in the offer.
cells.limitation: Section D lists disputes the debate settled (trial period, T10) or never had.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T2 restates T1's vivid-versus-dull claim accurately before challenging it.
cells.limitation: T2 says T1 treats the commute as certain; T1 claimed undercounting, not certainty.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T9 names the review date's assumed neutrality and how it fails; T10 answers it.
cells.limitation: T12's objection to T11 rests on an unargued generalisation about flattery.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: Three hours a day from 90 minutes each way is correct arithmetic (Section A).
cells.limitation: T12 asserts flattery usually hides a hunger to grow, with no support.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T5 labels T4's door 'also a guess'; T11 offers motives as alternatives.
cells.limitation: T12 states a general psychological pattern as settled fact.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T3 'Fair hit, I'll narrow it' concedes the raise is real and rescopes the claim.
cells.limitation: The Bias Auditor never answers T4's claim that money-for-hours is the wrong ledger.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A says the gaps matter more than the percentage and names them.
cells.limitation: Why the user is weighing offers, or how the current job feels, is never asked.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T3 asks what 25% means after tax and travel costs.
cells.limitation: The 25% and three daily hours are never combined into an effective hourly comparison.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section D: 'Deciding how to rank time against income is yours to do.'
cells.limitation: T4's growth frame is the speaker's priority; the user stated none.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: Section E: sleep, health or caring duties may outweigh the money regardless.
cells.limitation: Section A says the offer 'adds' 90 minutes though the current commute is unknown.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on usable time, hybrid days and role advancement, with implications.
cells.limitation: Current commute length, flagged missing in Section A, never becomes a branch.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T11 offers money pressure, fear or flattery, says what each implies, 'not my call'.
cells.limitation: T12 then nudges toward one motive with a general claim about flattery.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T5: people tell flattering stories about where a job will lead.
cells.limitation: The assumption that the current job is a stable baseline is never examined.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: Section A sets money and security against time, health and the rest of life.
cells.limitation: Values are listed, not tested against a concrete sacrifice the user could weigh.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T11 names fear the offer won't recur; T9 names routine making quitting hard.
cells.limitation: Expectations from partner, family or peers never come up.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section D asks whether the strongest pull is money, fear of missing out, or the work.
cells.limitation: Section D's closing question repeats T11 rather than adding a new distinction.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: T12 adds a nearer job as an alternative road to growth.
cells.limitation: Negotiating remote days or pay, or a counteroffer, never appears as an option.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T3: the commute cost recurs daily; the raise shrinks after tax and travel.
cells.limitation: The cost of declining is touched only through T4's door, never weighed.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: five fixed driving days versus usable hybrid time, each with the option favoured.
cells.limitation: 'A much bigger gain than 25%' (T8, Section E) is never sized from the user's hours.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section E lists true office days, net pay, a route trial and a role conversation.
cells.limitation: Minor unknowns are not explicitly separated from the consequential ones.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: T5 rush-hour trial, T6 talk to someone in the role, T10 written exit conditions.
cells.limitation: The review date in T8 is never given a basis for its timing.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T7: a train where you read versus 'a car where you grind your teeth'.
cells.limitation: T12's 'flattery rarely stays alone' is compressed and slightly opaque.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T5 'Your door' and T9 'Your review date' point clearly to T4 and T8.
cells.limitation: T12 'I'd dispute the order' is ambiguous; Section D misattributes open disputes.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Twelve turns, all within 25 to 65 words per the deterministic checks.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: Each mind holds a distinct lens: bias, bet pricing, identity trajectory.
cells.limitation: All three share one calm, measured register by mid-debate (T6 onward).

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: Section E adds sleep and caring duties beyond T8's branches.
cells.limitation: Section E largely repeats the branches of T7 and T8.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T4: 'a pay cut disguised as a raise' if the job is the same.
cells.limitation: Daily-life costs stay abstract; no evening, family or sleep picture is drawn.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T10 concedes to T9's sunk-routine point and says how it improves the plan.
cells.limitation: Reversals in T3 and T10 are modest narrowings; none surprises.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T1 opens bluntly: 'this is a trap built for human brains.'
cells.limitation: Bettor and Trajectory Critic lose distinct flavour after T6.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T4 'the commute is a toll'; T10 'Pre-commitment is cheaper than willpower later.'
cells.limitation: Few concrete images beyond T7's car and train.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T9 turns the agreed review date into a hidden trap.
cells.limitation: Even intensity throughout; T12 ends on a new question without payoff.

strengths: T9 and T10: the review-date objection and pre-written exit conditions develop the plan through real concession.
Section E gives observable branches (office days, usable time, role advancement), each with the option it favours.
T11 offers three motives as alternatives with implications and leaves the judgment to the user.
weaknesses: No mind raises negotiating hybrid days, pay or a counteroffer; options stay accept, test or decline (T5, T12).
The 25% and three daily hours are never turned into an hourly comparison (T3, Section E).
Section D reports disagreements the debate settled (T10) or never had, blurring what remains open.

symptoms.observed: Negotiating remote days, pay or a counteroffer never appears among the options.
symptoms.evidence: asking how often the team is in person?

symptoms.observed: The user's two numbers are never combined into an effective hourly comparison.
symptoms.evidence: 25% of what, after tax and travel costs?

symptoms.evidence: The minds still disagree about how much to trust your forecast

symptoms.observed: T12 states a general psychological pattern about flattery as fact.
symptoms.evidence: Flattery rarely stays alone for long; it usually hides a hunger

symptoms.observed: Rhythm stays even; the debate ends on a fresh question with no payoff.

findings.description: Asserts that flattery usually hides a hunger to grow, with no support or hedge.
Says the minds still disagree on adaptation and the trial period; T10 conceded and adaptation was never disputed.
Says the offer adds 90 minutes each way; the user gave the total commute, and the current commute is unknown.
Commute non-adaptation attributed to Kahneman's mind and pre-commitment to Duke's; consistent with memory, not checkable here.

rubric_fit_notes: The user gave only two facts, so C3 cells weigh branching on gaps more than use of context. Uncertain whether the missing negotiation option is material or minor.
question_type_note: Decision type: all cells read as written, with options and thresholds judged against accepting or declining this offer.
